title: Germs and How We Fight Them
bigQuestion: Germs are too small to see, so how do our bodies, our habits and our medicines keep us well?

story.title: The Milkmaid's Clear Skin
story.kicker: An old country story helped a doctor find a way to stop one of the worst sicknesses in history.
paragraphs: Long ago in the English countryside, a sickness called smallpox scared almost everyone. It gave people a high fever and bumpy spots all over the skin. Many people died from it. Many who got well had scars on their faces for life.

Edward Jenner was a country doctor in the village of Berkeley, England. Farm families there told an old story. They said milkmaids who caught a mild sickness from cows almost never got smallpox. That cow sickness was called cowpox. It gave a milkmaid a few sores on her hands, and then she got well.

One well-known telling says a young milkmaid spoke to Jenner herself. She said she would never catch smallpox, because she had already had cowpox. Nobody knows her exact words. But Jenner kept thinking about the idea. Could a mild cow sickness protect a person from a deadly one?

In 1796 Jenner decided to test it. He took a little matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes. He put it into a small cut on the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. James got a little sick and then got better.

Weeks later, Jenner exposed James to smallpox. James did not get sick. Jenner tested more people and wrote down what he saw. His work led to the first vaccine. Doctors today would never test on a child that way, but his idea changed the world.
story.think: Jenner heard a story, then tested it. Why is it important to test an idea instead of just believing a story?

lessons.title: Bacteria Are Tiny Living Things
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria are tiny one-celled living things; most are harmless or helpful, but a few can make us sick.
reading: Think about a spoonful of yogurt. It is full of living things, too small to see. They are called *bacteria*. Each one is just a single cell. You would need a microscope to see them.
Bacteria live almost everywhere. They live in soil, in water and on your skin. Millions live inside your gut. Most bacteria do not hurt you. Many help you digest food or turn milk into yogurt.
A few kinds of bacteria are *germs*. A germ is a tiny living thing that can make you sick. One kind of bacteria causes strep throat. Another kind can get into a cut and make it red and sore.

words.d: tiny living things made of just one cell; most are harmless, and a few cause sickness
tiny living things, like some bacteria and viruses, that can make you sick

look.title: A Look Through a Microscope
look.text: A student puts a drop of pond water under a microscope. At first she sees nothing. Then she turns the knob. Tiny rods and dots appear, far too small to see with her eyes alone.
look.prompt: Why did people not know about bacteria until they had microscopes?

check.q: What are bacteria?
check.why: The reading says bacteria are tiny living things made of just one cell.

check.q: Which is true about most bacteria?
choices: They are big enough to see.
check.why: Most bacteria do not hurt you, and many help, like the ones that make yogurt.

check.q: Which sickness is caused by a kind of bacteria?
check.why: The reading names strep throat as a sickness caused by bacteria.

lessons.title: Viruses Need a Host
lessons.mainIdea: Viruses are even smaller than bacteria, and they can only make more of themselves inside a living cell.
reading: When you catch a cold, a *virus* is usually the cause. A virus is a germ even smaller than bacteria. The flu and chickenpox are also caused by viruses.

A virus cannot grow or make copies on its own. It must get inside a living cell. The cell it uses is called the *host*. Inside, the virus makes the cell build many new viruses. Then they spread to more cells.
Bacteria and viruses are both germs, but they are different. Bacteria are living cells. Viruses are much smaller and are not cells at all. This difference matters when doctors choose a medicine.

words.d: a very tiny germ that can only make copies of itself inside a living cell
the living thing or cell that a virus uses to make copies of itself

look.title: How Small Are Germs?
look.prompt: About how many bacteria could line up across one hair? Which germ is the smallest?

check.q: What must a virus do to make copies of itself?
choices: Split in half on its own
check.why: A virus can only make copies inside a living cell, its host.

check.q: Which is usually caused by a virus?
check.why: The reading says colds are usually caused by viruses.

check.q: How are viruses different from bacteria?
choices: Viruses are much smaller and are not cells.
check.why: Bacteria are living cells; viruses are much smaller and are not cells.

lessons.title: How Germs Travel
lessons.mainIdea: Germs spread through the air, by touch, and in food and water, so washing hands and covering coughs help.
reading: Maya sneezes into the air. Tiny drops fly out. If she has a cold, the drops carry the virus. A friend nearby can breathe them in. That is one way germs *spread*.

Germs also spread by touch. Someone coughs into a hand, then touches a door handle. The next person touches it and then rubs an eye. Germs can also ride in food that was not cooked well, or in dirty water.

Simple habits block these paths. Wash hands with soap and water for about 20 seconds. Cough or sneeze into your elbow. Keep food clean and cooked. Drink clean water. These habits cut down the chances of getting sick. This is called good *hygiene*.

words.d: to pass from one person or place to another
habits that keep you and others clean and healthy, like washing hands

look.title: Washing Hands the Right Way
look.text: Wet your hands with clean running water. Add soap and rub every part, including the backs and between the fingers, for at least 20 seconds. Rinse well and dry with a clean towel or air dry.
look.cite: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), When and How to Wash Your Hands, handwashing guidance
look.prompt: Why do you think the CDC says to scrub for 20 seconds and not just a quick splash?

check.q: Which is one way germs spread?
check.why: Sneezes send out tiny drops that can carry germs through the air.

check.q: How long should you scrub hands with soap?
check.why: The reading and the CDC say to scrub for about 20 seconds.

check.q: Where is the best place to sneeze if you have no tissue?
check.why: Sneezing into your elbow keeps germs off your hands and out of the air.

lessons.title: White Blood Cells on Guard
lessons.mainIdea: The immune system uses white blood cells to find and destroy germs that get into the body.
reading: Your skin is like a wall that keeps most germs out. But sometimes germs get in, like through a scrape on your knee. Then your body has a team ready to fight. That team is your *immune system*.

The fighters are *white blood cells*. They travel in your blood to where germs are. Some white blood cells swallow germs whole. Others make *antibodies*. Antibodies are like tags that stick to a germ so other cells can find it and destroy it.

Your immune system also remembers. After it beats a germ, some cells keep a memory of it. If the same germ comes back, your body can fight it faster. This memory is why many people get chickenpox only once.

words.d: the body's team of cells and organs that fights germs
blood cells that find and fight germs
tiny tags the body makes that stick to one kind of germ so it can be destroyed

look.title: The Scraped Knee
look.text: Leo scrapes his knee on the playground. The next day the spot is a little pink and warm. A few days later it has healed. Under the skin, white blood cells rushed in to clean up germs.
look.prompt: What was happening inside Leo's knee while it healed?

check.q: What is the job of white blood cells?
choices: To carry food to the stomach
check.why: White blood cells travel to germs and fight them.

check.q: What do antibodies do?
choices: Stick to a germ so it can be destroyed
check.why: Antibodies are like tags that stick to one kind of germ.

check.q: Why do many people get chickenpox only once?
choices: The immune system remembers the germ.
check.why: The immune system keeps a memory of germs it has beaten and fights them faster next time.

lessons.title: A Fever Is a Fight
lessons.mainIdea: A fever is a higher body temperature that often means the immune system is fighting germs.
reading: Ana wakes up hot and tired. Her dad checks her with a thermometer. Her temperature is higher than usual. She has a *fever*. Her dad tucks her back into bed with a glass of water.

A fever is not a germ. It is one way your body fights germs. When germs get in, the body turns up its heat. Some germs do not grow as well in a warmer body. The heat may also help the immune system work.
A fever can make you feel tired and achy. Resting and drinking water help. Tell a grown-up when you feel hot or sick. A grown-up can check your *temperature* and call a doctor or nurse if needed.

words.d: a body temperature higher than usual, often a sign the body is fighting germs
how hot or cold something is, measured with a thermometer

look.title: Reading a Thermometer
look.cite: CDC definition of fever (100.4 °F or higher); typical body temperature from common medical references
look.prompt: Ana's thermometer says 101. Does she have a fever? How do you know?

check.q: What is a fever?
choices: A body temperature higher than usual
check.why: A fever is a higher body temperature, often from fighting germs.

check.q: How can a fever help the body?
choices: Some germs do not grow as well in the heat.
check.why: The reading says some germs grow less well in a warmer body.

check.q: What should Ana do when she feels hot and sick?
check.why: Telling a grown-up and resting are the helpful steps in the reading.

lessons.title: How a Vaccine Works
lessons.mainIdea: A vaccine teaches the immune system to know a germ, so the body is ready before the real germ arrives.
reading: A fire drill helps you practice before there is a real fire. A *vaccine* is like a drill for your immune system. It lets the body practice fighting a germ without getting very sick.
A vaccine holds a weak, dead or harmless piece of a germ, or instructions for making one. It is often given as a shot. The immune system sees it and makes antibodies. It also makes memory cells.

Later, the real germ may come. Now the body knows it. It can fight fast, often before you feel sick. This protection is called *immunity*. Your doctor or nurse can tell you which vaccines you need and when.

words.d: a medicine, often a shot, that teaches the immune system to know a germ
the body's protection against a germ it already knows

look.title: The Practice Drill
look.text: At school, the fire alarm rings for a drill. Everyone walks out in a line. There is no fire. A month later, the class does it again, faster and calmer.
look.prompt: How is a fire drill like a vaccine? How is it different?

check.q: What does a vaccine do?
choices: Teaches the immune system to know a germ
Kills every germ in a room
check.why: A vaccine lets the immune system learn a germ before the real one comes.

check.q: What does a vaccine usually hold?
choices: A weak, dead or harmless piece of a germ, or instructions for one
check.why: The reading says vaccines hold a weak, dead or harmless part of a germ, or instructions to make one.

check.q: What is immunity?
choices: The body's protection against a germ it knows
check.why: Immunity is the body's protection against a germ it has learned.

lessons.title: Edward Jenner Tests an Idea
lessons.mainIdea: In 1796 Edward Jenner used cowpox to protect a boy from smallpox, which led to the first vaccine.
reading: *Smallpox* was a sickness caused by a virus. It killed many people for thousands of years. In the 1700s, English farm families noticed something. Milkmaids who had caught *cowpox* from cows seemed safe from smallpox.
Edward Jenner, a country doctor, tested this idea in 1796. He put matter from a cowpox sore into a cut on James Phipps's arm. Later, he exposed James to smallpox. James stayed well.
Jenner wrote a book about his tests in 1798. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Today, doctors test vaccines with careful rules to keep volunteers safe.

words.d: a deadly sickness caused by a virus that gave people fever and spots
a mild sickness from cows that protected people from smallpox

look.title: Jenner's Report
look.text: Jenner wrote that people who had caught cowpox from milking cows seemed to be protected from smallpox afterward. He described giving cowpox to a boy and then showing that the boy did not catch smallpox.
look.cite: Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, 1798
look.prompt: What did Jenner see, and what did he do to test it?

check.q: What did Jenner use to protect James Phipps?
check.why: Jenner used matter from a cowpox sore to protect James.

check.q: When did Jenner test his idea on James?
check.why: Jenner's test on James Phipps was in 1796.

check.q: Where does the word vaccine come from?
check.why: Vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow.

lessons.title: The End of Smallpox
lessons.mainIdea: Vaccines used all over the world wiped out smallpox, and in 1980 it was declared gone.
reading: After Jenner, many countries began to vaccinate people against smallpox. In 1967 the World Health Organization started a big push to end it everywhere. Health workers traveled to villages all over the world.
The workers found each new case. Then they vaccinated everyone around that sick person. This stopped the virus from finding new people. The last natural case was found in Somalia, in Africa, in 1977.
In 1980 the World Health Organization said smallpox was *eradicated*. That means it was wiped out in the wild. It is the first human disease ever wiped out. It took teamwork from many *nations*.

words.d: wiped out completely, so it no longer spreads anywhere
countries with their own governments

look.title: The World Says Smallpox Is Gone
look.text: In 1980 the World Health Assembly declared that the world and all its peoples had won freedom from smallpox. It thanked the nations and health workers who took part.
look.cite: World Health Assembly, resolution declaring the global eradication of smallpox, May 1980
look.prompt: Why do you think this was called a win for all the world's peoples?

check.q: What does eradicated mean?
check.why: Eradicated means wiped out so it no longer spreads.

check.q: In what year was smallpox declared gone?
check.why: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

check.q: How did health workers stop smallpox from spreading?
choices: They told people to stay in the sun.
They found each case and vaccinated people nearby.
check.why: Workers found cases and vaccinated people around them, so the virus ran out of new people.

lessons.title: Antibiotics Fight Bacteria
lessons.mainIdea: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing.
reading: In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming came back to his lab in London. He saw mold growing on a dish of bacteria. Around the mold, the bacteria had died. The mold made something that killed them.

That something became *penicillin*. It was one of the first *antibiotics*. An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing. Penicillin was made in large amounts in the 1940s and saved many lives.
Doctors give antibiotics for infections caused by bacteria, like strep throat. Only a doctor or nurse can decide if you need one. Take it just the way they say, and finish it if they tell you to.

words.d: medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing
one of the first antibiotics, first found in a mold

look.title: The Moldy Dish
look.text: Fleming's dish had a spot of fuzzy mold. All around it was a clear ring where bacteria were gone. Farther away, the bacteria grew thick.
look.prompt: What clue told Fleming that the mold was doing something to the bacteria?

check.q: Who noticed mold killing bacteria in 1928?
check.why: Alexander Fleming saw the mold in his London lab in 1928.

check.q: What is an antibiotic?
choices: A shot that teaches the body a germ
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops their growth
check.why: Antibiotics are medicines that work against bacteria.

check.q: Who decides if you need an antibiotic?
check.why: Only a doctor or nurse can decide if you need one.

lessons.title: Why Antibiotics Skip Viruses
lessons.mainIdea: Antibiotics work on bacteria but not on viruses, so they do not help a cold or the flu.
reading: Sam has a runny nose and a cough. He asks his doctor for an antibiotic. The doctor kindly says no. Sam's cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not work on viruses.
Antibiotics attack parts that bacteria have, like their cell walls. Viruses do not have those parts. So the medicine has nothing to hit. For a cold, rest, fluids and time usually help most.

Using antibiotics when they are not needed can cause a problem. Some bacteria learn to survive them. This is called antibiotic *resistance*. Using antibiotics only when a doctor says so helps keep them *effective* for everyone.

words.d: when germs change so a medicine no longer works on them
able to do the job it is supposed to do

look.title: Fleming's Warning
look.text: When Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize, he warned that if people took too little penicillin or took it when it was not needed, bacteria could learn to resist it.
look.prompt: Fleming found penicillin. Why would he warn people about using it the wrong way?

check.q: Why did Sam's doctor not give him an antibiotic?
choices: His cold was caused by a virus.
check.why: Antibiotics do not work on viruses, and colds are caused by viruses.

check.q: What is antibiotic resistance?
choices: When bacteria can survive a medicine
check.why: Resistance means germs change so the medicine no longer works.

check.q: What helps most for a cold?
check.why: The reading says rest, fluids and time usually help a cold most.

review.why: Bacteria are one-celled living things; viruses are not cells.

review.q: Which habit helps stop germs from spreading by touch?
review.why: Handwashing with soap removes germs from your hands.

review.q: What part of the body fights germs with white blood cells?
review.why: The immune system uses white blood cells to fight germs.

review.q: What story gave Edward Jenner his idea?
choices: Children who ate yogurt stayed well.
Doctors who washed hands stayed well.
People in cities never got sick.
Milkmaids who had cowpox seemed safe from smallpox.
review.why: Farm families said milkmaids with cowpox did not catch smallpox.

review.q: How is a vaccine different from an antibiotic?
choices: A vaccine teaches the body ahead of time; an antibiotic fights bacteria already there.
A vaccine kills bacteria; an antibiotic prevents viruses.
review.why: Vaccines prepare the immune system; antibiotics attack bacteria during an infection.

review.q: Which disease was the first ever wiped out worldwide?
A fever is best described as what?
choices: A sign the body is fighting germs
review.why: A fever is a higher temperature that often means the body is fighting.

review.q: Why should antibiotics be used only when a doctor says so?
review.why: Using them when not needed can help bacteria learn to survive them.
